ending: Shadow discovers that the war between old and new gods was never real. Wednesday, who is the American Odin, secretly conspired with the trickster Loki, who had been posing as both Shadow's old cellmate and the new gods' cold leader Mr. World, to provoke a battle in which the deaths of gods on both sides would become a great sacrifice, feeding the two of them and restoring their power. Wednesday's own murder was staged as the spark. Having died on the world-tree and returned from the dead, Shadow understands the con and confronts the gods massing for battle at Lookout Mountain, laying the whole scheme bare so that the assembled powers, cheated of their war, disperse rather than slaughter one another. Loki's plot collapses and both conspirators are undone. Shadow also learns the truth of his own origins: Wednesday fathered him as part of the long game, so the con man he served was his father. Afterward Shadow returns to Lakeside and solves its mystery, revealing that the beloved old Hinzelmann is a kobold who has kept the town safe and prosperous for generations by taking the life of one child every winter; exposed, Hinzelmann's hold ends. Freed of the gods' schemes and his grief for Laura settled, Shadow leaves America and travels to Iceland, where he meets the older, original Odin and, in a small final gesture, hands over a token, walking away lighter than he came.
in_short: Released from prison to the news that his wife Laura has died in a car crash, Shadow Moon takes a job as bodyguard for a charismatic con man calling himself Mr. Wednesday. Traveling America, Shadow discovers that the odd old people Wednesday visits are gods brought over by generations of immigrants, now faded and forgotten, and that Wednesday is Odin, rallying them for war against a rising pantheon of new gods of media, technology, and money. Laura returns from the grave, uncannily animate thanks to a magical coin Shadow was given, and repeatedly protects him. For his safety Shadow hides in the pleasant lakeside town of Lakeside, whose prosperity conceals a grim secret. When Wednesday is killed during a parley with the new gods, the old gods rally for battle, and Shadow keeps a death-vigil bound to a great tree, dying and passing to the land of the dead before returning. There he realizes the whole war is a con: Wednesday and his hidden partner Loki, disguised as the new gods' leader Mr. World, engineered it so the slaughter would be a sacrifice feeding them both. Shadow exposes the grift to the assembled gods and stops the battle. He also learns Wednesday was his father. He then returns to Lakeside and uncovers that the kindly old Hinzelmann has kept the town prosperous by sacrificing a child each winter, ending the arrangement before leaving to find a kind of peace abroad.

recaps.text: Days before his release from prison, Shadow Moon is told that his wife, Laura, has died in a car accident, and he leaves incarceration with nothing left to come home to. On the journey he keeps meeting a strange one-eyed old man calling himself Mr. Wednesday, who seems to know all about him and offers him work as a bodyguard and driver. With no better options, Shadow takes the job. Almost at once his new life turns uncanny: a foul-mouthed brawler claiming to be a leprechaun, Mad Sweeney, forces a magical gold coin on him, and a menacing young man surrounded by screens threatens him out of nowhere. At Laura's funeral Shadow learns a painful truth about how she died. Grieving and bewildered, he follows Wednesday into a country that is clearly stranger than it looks.

Traveling with Wednesday, Shadow is introduced to a widening circle of shabby, aging eccentrics, from a grim old hammer-wielding Slav named Czernobog and his sisters to a sly storytelling gentleman, Mr. Nancy, and scholarly undertakers in a river town. He gradually grasps the secret behind them: these are gods, carried to America in the hearts of immigrants over the centuries and now weakened and half-forgotten, and Wednesday is one of them, going from one to the next to recruit them for a coming war against a new breed of powers born of television, computers, and modern life. Laura, meanwhile, rises from her grave, cold and uncannily preserved but still herself, and begins appearing to protect Shadow. The new gods, led by figures like Media and the smooth Mr. World, make plain that they consider the old ones obsolete and want them gone, and Shadow finds himself a marked man.

As tensions mount, Wednesday stashes Shadow for safekeeping in Lakeside, a small, unusually pleasant and prosperous town in the far north, where he lives quietly under a false name and is welcomed by the locals, especially a warm, story-spinning old man named Hinzelmann. Shadow comes to like the place, though he notices an unsettling pattern: every winter a child vanishes from the town without explanation. Between spells in Lakeside he keeps helping Wednesday, who continues gathering the old gods and pressing them toward open conflict, holding councils and forging alliances. Laura drifts in and out of Shadow's life, still watching over him from beyond death, while the standoff with the new gods sharpens toward violence and Shadow is drawn ever deeper into a war he only partly understands.

The conflict finally breaks. During what is supposed to be a truce and negotiation with the new gods, Wednesday is shot and killed, an act that outrages the old gods and drives them toward all-out war, with Shadow now bound up in their cause. Honoring a promise he made to Wednesday, Shadow agrees to hold the old man's death-vigil, and is tied to a great ash tree to keep watch. There, exposed and without food or water, he suffers, weakens, and dies, his spirit passing out of the world entirely and into the realm of the dead, where he faces a reckoning of his life and of everything he has done and been. The gods, meanwhile, gather their forces for a decisive battle, believing Wednesday a martyr to their cause.

Shadow returns from death with the truth in hand: the war is a swindle. Wednesday, the American Odin, and the trickster Loki, who has been posing as Shadow's former cellmate and as the new gods' leader Mr. World, staged the entire conflict so that a battlefield full of dying gods would become a sacrifice restoring both conspirators to power; Wednesday even engineered his own killing as the trigger, and had fathered Shadow as part of the plan. Shadow reaches the assembled armies at Lookout Mountain and exposes the con, so that the cheated gods break off rather than fight, and Loki's scheme falls apart. With the crisis past and his grief for Laura finally laid to rest, Shadow goes back to Lakeside and unravels its secret, revealing that the kindly Hinzelmann is an ancient household spirit who has bought the town's prosperity by sacrificing one child every winter for generations; once he is exposed, the bargain ends. Free at last, Shadow leaves the country and travels to Iceland, where he meets the old original Odin and, in a quiet parting gesture, walks away unburdened.
